items.stemHtml:
A 54-year-old man has had 3 months of a painless purplish rash on both lower legs, joint aches and fatigue. Blood pressure is 148/90 mmHg. There is palpable purpura on the shins. Laboratory studies:

TestResult
Serum creatinine1.4 mg/dL (baseline 1.0 mg/dL a year ago)
Urine protein-to-creatinine ratio1.2 g/g
Urine microscopyDysmorphic red cells, occasional red cell casts
C3Mildly low
C4Very low
Rheumatoid factorStrongly positive
Hepatitis C virus RNADetectable
HBsAg, HIV antibody, ANCA, anti-dsDNANegative

Kidney function has been stable over the past 2 weeks. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.label: A
options.html: Direct-acting antiviral therapy against hepatitis C

items.explanationHtml:
Purpura, arthralgia, very low C4 with a lesser fall in C3, a strongly positive rheumatoid factor (the IgM component of type II cryoglobulins) and HCV viremia point to mixed cryoglobulinemia with membranoproliferative GN from hepatitis C. When kidney function is stable and the disease is not rapidly progressive or organ-threatening, the first step is to treat the driver with direct-acting antivirals, which often lead to remission. Rituximab (with or without plasma exchange) is added for severe or rapidly progressive disease.

Takeaway: HCV cryoglobulinemic GN that is not rapidly progressive: start direct-acting antivirals first; add rituximab only for severe disease.

whyNot.B: Cyclophosphamide and high-dose steroids increase HCV replication and are reserved, if used at all, for severe vasculitis not controlled otherwise.
whyNot.C: Interferon-based therapy is outdated; it is less effective, poorly tolerated and can worsen vasculitis.
whyNot.D: Plasma exchange removes cryoglobulins in life-threatening disease (rapidly progressive GN, hyperviscosity) but does not treat the cause.
whyNot.E: Rituximab with or without plasma exchange is for severe, organ-threatening disease; his kidney function is stable, so antiviral therapy comes first.

items.objective: Treat HCV-associated cryoglobulinemic glomerulonephritis with direct-acting antivirals when it is not rapidly progressive.
